summary: Third John is a personal letter from “the elder” to Gaius, whom he praises for walking in truth and helping travelling brothers, including strangers. The elder asks Gaius to continue sending such workers onward, contrasts that support with Diotrephes’s refusal and exclusion of others, and then commends Demetrius. The letter closes with the elder’s hope to speak face to face and with greetings among friends.
whyItMatters: The chapter shows how truth and love become visible in concrete treatment of people: welcome, support, refusal, accusation, and exclusion. It also preserves a local conflict without giving every side of the dispute, so the reader must notice both the force of the elder’s appeal and the limits of what the letter tells us.

context.author: The writer identifies himself only as “the elder.” Christian tradition attributes the letter to John the apostle, while some scholars consider another leader in the Johannine circle possible.
context.audience: Gaius, an individual praised for helping fellow believers, including strangers; the letter also refers to an assembly, travelling brothers, Diotrephes, Demetrius, and friends.
context.date: Often placed near the end of the first century CE, though the letter itself gives no date.
context.setting: The location is not named. Ephesus or its surrounding region in Asia Minor is a proposed setting, not something stated in the address.
context.literaryForm: A short personal letter with praise, a practical request, an accusation against Diotrephes, a recommendation of Demetrius, and a closing hope for a visit.

outline.heading: Greeting to Gaius
outline.note: The elder addresses Gaius as beloved and speaks of loving him in truth.

outline.heading: Joy over Gaius’s truth
outline.note: The elder prays for Gaius’s well-being and rejoices over reports that he walks in truth.

outline.heading: Support for travelling brothers
outline.note: Gaius is praised for faithful work toward brothers and strangers, and the elder urges him to send them forward in a way worthy of God.

outline.heading: Diotrephes’s resistance
outline.note: The elder says Diotrephes rejects him, speaks against him, refuses the brothers, and excludes those who would receive them.

outline.heading: Imitate good, and Demetrius commended
outline.note: Gaius is urged not to imitate evil but good, and Demetrius is supported by testimony from all, from the truth, and from the elder’s circle.

outline.heading: Ink, visit, and greetings
outline.note: The elder leaves many things for a hoped-for face-to-face meeting and closes with peace and greetings among friends.

keyVerses.text: I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the elder’s joy and names the conduct that frames his praise of Gaius.

keyVerses.text: We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
keyVerses.why: This gives the reason for supporting the travellers: receiving them makes others partners in their work for the truth.

keyVerses.text: Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, he doesn’t receive the brothers himself, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly.
keyVerses.why: This is the fullest statement of the elder’s charge against Diotrephes and explains the practical conflict in the letter.

keyVerses.text: Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God.
keyVerses.why: This turns the conflict into a direct moral appeal about what kind of conduct Gaius should copy.

questions.question: Who is “the elder”?
questions.answer: The letter’s writer gives this title instead of a personal name. Later Christian tradition connects the letter with John the apostle, while some readers think another leader in the Johannine circle may be meant. The chapter itself does not settle the identification.

questions.question: Who is Gaius?
questions.answer: Gaius is the recipient of the letter and is called beloved. The elder praises him because others have reported that he walks in truth and because he has helped brothers and strangers. The chapter does not give enough information to identify him securely with another person named Gaius elsewhere.

questions.question: What does “walk in truth” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, walking in truth is something other people can testify about in Gaius’s conduct. It is not described as a physical journey; it is a way of living that fits the truth the elder values. The phrase prepares for the practical request to receive and support the travellers.

questions.question: Does verse 2 promise health and prosperity to every believer?
questions.answer: Verse 2 is a prayer in a personal greeting to Gaius. The elder asks that Gaius may prosper and be healthy, comparing that wish with the prospering of his soul. The wording is not presented as a universal guarantee about wealth or health.

questions.question: Who are the “brothers and strangers”?
questions.answer: They are travelling fellow believers whom Gaius has helped, even though some were strangers to him. The elder says they have testified about Gaius’s love before the assembly. Their travel and dependence on support are central to the request in verses 5-8.

questions.question: What does “the Name” refer to?
questions.answer: Verse 7 says the travellers went out “for the sake of the Name,” taking nothing from the Gentiles. USCCB’s note identifies the Name with Jesus Christ, though the verse itself leaves the expression unexpanded. The travellers’ work and lack of support from the Gentiles ground the following appeal for fellow believers to receive them.

questions.question: What exactly did Diotrephes do wrong?
questions.answer: The elder says Diotrephes loves to be first, does not accept what the elder says, accuses them with wicked words, refuses to receive the brothers, forbids others who want to receive them, and throws those people out of the assembly. This is the elder’s account of the conflict. Diotrephes’s own explanation is not preserved in the chapter.

questions.question: Why is Demetrius mentioned?
questions.answer: Demetrius is commended by testimony from all, from the truth itself, and from the elder’s group. He may have carried the letter, as USCCB’s note suggests, but the chapter does not state his role. The recommendation gives Gaius reason to trust him.

questions.question: Why does the elder prefer speaking “face to face”?
questions.answer: The elder says he has many things to write but is unwilling to continue with ink and pen. He hopes to see Gaius soon and speak face to face. The closing shows that the letter is part of an ongoing relationship and that some matters are being left for a personal visit.

glossary.def: The title the writer uses for himself in verse 1; it marks him as a recognized figure but does not give his personal name.
The beloved recipient of the letter, praised for walking in truth and for helping travelling brothers and strangers.
The gathered community mentioned in connection with testimony about Gaius and with Diotrephes’s exclusion of others.
The people from whom the travellers took nothing in verse 7; the letter contrasts taking support from them with receiving support from fellow believers.
The person the elder accuses of rejecting his message, refusing the brothers, and throwing supporters out of the assembly.
The man commended in verse 12 by testimony from all, from the truth itself, and from the elder’s circle.
